title: Eldfall Chronicles: Apocrypha is Live!
content:
The Gamefound campaign for Eldfall Chronicles: Apocrypha is live!

Amidst the roaring dunes, along the banks of the Ashara River, stands one of the greatest wonders of the known world—the Grand Library, encircled by the capital of the Sand Kingdoms. A monolithic tower, said to predate mortal civilizations, it rises tenfold higher than any structure built by human hands. Beneath it lie the Sealed Archives, rumored to hold knowledge from the ages of the Elders and the Gods.

Three years after the events of the Northern Wind expedition, the echoes of the calamity that split Mt. Byodo have begun to stir once more. After centuries of silence, something within the Archives has awakened.

For the first time in recorded history, the Librarian, an enigmatic curator of the Library, has called upon mortals to retrieve what was lost. Now, all eyes turn to the capital of the Sand Kingdoms, as the hunt for the Apocrypha within the Sealed Archives begins.

Credit: Freecompany

Eldfall Chronicles: Apocrypha is a cooperative dungeon crawl for 1-4 players combining a narrative storyline, tactical combat, high quality miniatures, and replayability due to branching paths and mechanics to keep things changing. There are multiple pledge levels available starting with the Core Pledge that includes a few miniatures and plenty of standees – for a preview of some of that content, check out our review of Apocrypha that went live yesterday. Other levels include more miniatures, additional story arcs, various bits of swag, and even a Dungeon Crawl All-In level that gets you not only the new Apocrypha release but also all of the Northern Wind releases from their past crowd funder.

Continuing the trend of all of the Eldfall Chronicles releases, Eldfall Chronicles: Apocrypha is fully compatible with their other dungeon crawl games as well as skirmish wargame mode of playing.

title: Steel Platoon first impressions - hardcore real time tactics
content:
Steel Platoon was revealed on Saturday, a real time tactics game set in WW2 with a fifteen mission single-player campaign following the Russian defense in the battle of Moscow. Thanks to an invitation from publisher Slitherine Software I was able to get my hands on an early build of the game at Games Ground Convention in Berlin - here are my thoughts.

Developed by new studio Tactical Move, Steel Platoon seems to be built on the same engine as Slitherine's Terminator: Dark Fate Defiance. Destructible terrain, modelled vehicle armor, ammunition and fuel tracking, squads of infantry you control as one, special abilities and gear tied to hot keys, it's all there. TDFD is far from the most famous game, probably because it's stuck with the Terminator franchise's least popular sub-license, but it's a deep real time tactics title. Shifting the setting to WW2 could be a crowd-pleasing move.

While multiplayer is promised, Saturday's announcement (and the demo build) focused on the fifteen mission single-player campaign. This has RPG-like progression elements, with a persistent force that grows and shrinks between missions, and troops who gain experience and specialisms (or die permanently). The protagonists are all invented boots-on-the-ground soldiers, not famous generals, and it's possible for them to die in the course of battles, which will apparently affect how the story unfolds.

How much the story will branch is yet unclear, and it will be vital. I love the fantasy of an army that persists between missions, but designers need to account for the possibility that you'll win a mission so poorly that you go into the next one with a crippled army, or risk soft-locking players. It's particularly pernicious when a late difficulty spike punishes you for the outcome of a battle much earlier in the campaign.

Missions follow the battle for Moscow from the perspective of the Russian. According to the presentation for the game during the Slitherine Next livestream, objectives in the early campaign will include defense in depth, preserving troops during a retreat, or holding at any cost in the face of a German breakthrough. As Operation Barbarossa stalls to a halt in the teeth of staunch opposition and the lethal Russian winter, I have to assume they'll swing more towards offense.

The first campaign mission is a hectic multi-front defense set in a small city on the German army's route into Moscow. As different German elements close from all side your platoon is sent racing around the city, repelling thrusts from all angles, before you're eventually forced to retreat.

The characters are pure pulp. Your command squad includes a plucky youngster full of propaganda and courage, a grandfatherly veteran of the Finnish war, and a square-jawed lieutenant who is the de facto protagonist. The story is a straightforward tale of heroism, with your platoon fighting off German assaults and rescuing civilians, ending when your lieutenant bids farewell to his nurse sweetheart as your forces are recalled to Moscow.

The mission aims for cinema. It's packed with NPC units, with men dying in droves, buildings collapsing, tanks bursting into flames, and sub-objectives failed without ending the mission. Mission objectives could have been communicated more clearly - once you'd completed the set-piece in a location you could run onto the next one with all your forces, even if the AI defenders who came to relieve you did a rubbish job. But by not breaking the action to inject new objectives, it felt like one breathless battle scene.

It was a little too much for my turn-based brain, and I rapidly found my force strung out throughout the city with no clear sense.  The minimap was too small for the density of unit icons, at least for my skill level, and I wished the camera could pan and descend so I could see further ahead of my troops to get a more geographically oriented view of the battlefield.

Better familiarity with the control scheme and the icons on the squad list - annoyingly placed top right of the screen instead of bottom centre as nature intended - would have helped. Overall, that first mission feels like the start of an action game where you're handed all of the end game abilities so you can feel really powerful, only to lose them once the story really starts. In a strategy game context, I found that every bit as bewildering as engaging.

The sheer quantity of units in the introductory mission, and the constant support of NPC units, also obfuscates just how important tactical positioning is to your success. Infantry need to take cover, or better yet garrison buildings, to survive sustained fire. Vehicles have individually modelled armor panels and breakable systems, and if a tank ever loses its crew because they die or they're forced to bail out, another crew can hop in to capture it.

The second campaign mission explores this in depth. You start with just two tanks, and have to loot fuel and ammo from German-controlled depots, then break out captured tank crews from captivity and retrieve an abandoned heavy tank. Set in snow-blanketed Russian countryside on a road between light rural settlements, you'd think this would fix my  problems with cognitive overload from the first mission. But two tanks proved more than enough for me to pilot - I didn't manage to break through this mission during the time I had available.

That could be balancing or AI, but at least some of it was me not knowing what I was doing - if I want to make that a developer problem, lets call it a failure of tutorialization. The less built up environment at least gave me plenty of room to admire the destructible terrain, stray shells turning wooden buildings into kindling, suggesting all sorts of tactical possibilities for creating angles of attack with heavy ordnance that I am currently too dumb to achieve.

I'm calling this one "promising", then: a solid singleplayer campaign set during WW2 is always welcome, destructible terrain and directional damage models are my kink, and as a miniature wargamer I'm a fiend for strategy games that skip out on real time base building. But I'm not yet convinced of the balancing or how accessible the control scheme is - I need more time to tell if the challenges I had with the demo were alpha jank, a skill gap on my part, or the intended experience.

It's been a while since Wargamer updated our guide to the best RTS games, and we haven't really grasped the nettle of what to do with real time tactics games - there's more and more of them every year. If you've got an opinion on whether or not we can mix the two - and which RTT's deserve to be on the list - let us know in the Wargamer Discord community.

title: Vampire the Masquerade's new playtest ditches most-hated mechanic and gives more power to the GM
content:
On Monday, White Wolf released the second playtest for Vampire: The Masquerade's 6th edition, dropping the Alpha 2.0 playtest alongside a dev diary to help explain the new changes. This new edition of the gothic TTRPG set in the World of Darkness has been pretty controversial so far, but given that 2.0 is subtitled: Changing Course, it looks like the creators are well aware of that and making changes in response to feedback.

The biggest point White Wolf has tried to address in this new version is giving Storytellers more to do. While the first version tried to reduce Storyteller load and give players more control and choices, the diaries suggest it leaned too hard in that direction.

The new version lets Storytellers roll for NPCs, and just generally gives them more to do. For instance, instead of players deciding on Devil's Bargains, conditions they can suffer as a way out of a failed roll, these are now offered by the Storyteller, who takes on the role of the Beast and offers a Faustian bargain.

Furthermore, while Choose Your Pain gave PCs difficult and interesting choices to make, White Wolf has now decided that letting players pick their poison "took the teeth out of failing". This is another choice that's been knocked back to the Storyteller's side of the court.

As well as expanding the Storytellers role, one of the other main changes is the stripping away of Drama and Quickening, two narrative-based metacurrencies that were a focus of the criticism around the first playtest.

Drama was intended to create a sense of shared story, but in practice it hampered more than helped, overcomplicating the practice of running games and restricting the Storyteller from imposing challenges as they saw fit.

Quickening, meanwhile, was a way for characters to push their powers to the limits, but in implementation this resource built up too quickly and made players feel too heroic for a horror game - obtaining power with no real cost.

Now Drama is gone for good (White Wolf says it could come back as a guidance tool for newbies) and players can spend Willpower to boost their chances on an important roll.

Our editor Mollie got on surprisingly well demoing the first Alpha playtest, praising its streamlined system, humanity scale, and the now scrapped Choose Your Pain mechanic. I think she'll be pleased to hear they've ditched the metacurrencies though.

We've not had time yet to dive into the new playtest and explore its changes. If you have, we'd love to hear your thoughts - come join our Discord.

title: Magic: The Gathering Star Trek Review, Part 1 of 4 - The Mechanics
content:
Space, the final frontier. These are the voyages of the starship Enterprise...as well as around 34 other new Spacecraft. Our continuing mission: To explore in detail the ramifications of newly-printed cardboard; to speculate upon their effects on formats such as Commander, Standard, & Modern; to boldly joke about the 43 new Creature types printed in this set unlikely ever to be seen again! Yes, Star Trek has arrived to Magic, and with it a host of new cards sure to shake things up. Most impactful is the full realization of Spacecraft as an Artifact subtype, more than doubling the number thusly printed. This week, we're covering the set's mechanics, with thrilling new abilities like a new spin on Flashback, and 'Creature types matter'. Jokes aside, many of the mechanics are quite dense for what is ostensibly a new-player-friendly set!

Star Trek officially releases to tabletop on November 13th, and on Magic: The Gathering Arena on November 10th.

New Mechanics

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Beam Me Up

Beam me up is a new spin on Flashback, appearing on Sorceries as an alternative cost. By returning a Creature you control to the hand as part of the cost, you can cast the Spell from your graveyard, with it being exiled as it leaves the stack. Importantly, like Web-slinging, the Creature is returned as soon as the Spell hits the stack, meaning this mechanic can be used as a way to protect or reset bodies without fear of interference.

Saffgor: Importantly, no Instant was printed with this mechanic in the set, and that's for good reason—if you could cast any of these in response to a removal Spell, they're essentially protection from the yard. That means they have a massive upside in any deck which can enable Flash, or a dedicated Scotty, Miracle Worker Commander deck using Instants. Including a couple of these in your list also makes you far less vulnerable to cards like Darksteel Mutation, with an inbuilt way to 'reset' your neutered Commander, and it appearing across all five colors introduces self-bounce to archetypes which would otherwise lack it. Neat stuff, though the name could have easily just been 'Beam Up' to make it readily reprintable.

BPhillipYork: I don't really like mechanics where what is happening doesn't really make any sense, sort of logically. In terms of balance this is just a flashback variant, it is decently set up so that you can build around it with creatures that get a lot of value from their ETB, or do weirder things like steal creatures then return them to your opponents hands somehow. Returning a creature to your hand is perfectly in synch with "beam me up" but then getting extra value from a spell is... weird? Anyway if you can get flash, or run Scotty, Miracle Worker this can get pretty abusive as a way to dodge removal, and all in all it's a fun mechanically slightly different flashback.

FromTheShire: We love a good flashback spell, and tacking on a way to bounce a creature back to your hand is very solid with the current state of enters triggers. I agree it's a bummer it got printed with a very parasitic name though.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Dilemmas

Dilemmas are a codified game action like Crimes, and you face a Dilemma when you choose one or more modes for a Spell or ability. That boils down to cards which have the 'Choose one —' syntax, followed by a bulleted list, but you can see a deeper breakdown in our article on Dilemmas from last week. Triggers that occur when you face a Dilemma go on the stack as soon as the modes are selected, above the triggering Spell or ability.

Saffgor: Dilemmas are substantially harder to face repeatedly compared to Crimes, but the fact many of their triggers lack guardrails like 'once per turn' does cause one to wonder. I've unironically been considering Pyramids in the big '26, as a mana outlet that faces a Dilemma, so I hope they print some more repeatable triggers soon. There's just not a ton of cards in the set which want you to face Dilemmas, and they're all either 5c or within the Blue and/or Black color identity; this means you're restricted from really paying off mass dilemmas unless you choose one of 3-4 middling Commanders.

BPhillipYork: I really like the idea of a trigger off of modal spells, because I think modal spells are neat. With only 10 dilemmas unless you are building around one of the two legendaries, though Captain Benjamin Sisko is actually pretty abusable and is easily the default dilemma commander. I hope they keep this as a deciduous or evergreen mechanic since I think modal spells help ease some of the built in frustration of magic, and it's a solid but balanced mechanic with a lot of potential design space.

FromTheShire: I'll be honest, I would have sworn this was already a keyword that existed. I'm sure I was just mashing up Riku of Many Paths and Villainous Choices in my head, but yeah, this is an easy space to fill. Thankfully it also doesn't have a Star Trek specific name so we can actually see this get expanded in the future. While there isn't a ton of support currently, this is one of those mechanics that has the potential to spike prices and become a whole thing years down the road.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Assimilate

Assimilate targets a Creature card in a specified zone, and moves them to your battlefield as a Borg Artifact Creature that enters/gains a +1/+1 counter, losing all other creature types. Recall that this all occurs on Layer 4, as type-changing effects, with the Assimilated quality being a single effect that alters both type and subtype. Assimilate cards in the set do so from the opposing battlefield, graveyard, and even exile, meaning resistance to the mechanic really is rather futile.

Saffgor: When I see a type-changing effect I know I'm in for a treat, being the resident Princess Yue guy here on Tabletop Battles. Assimilate notably only overwrites solely subtypes, and not supertypes, meaning if a card is Legendary it remains Legendary, or Land (e.g. Dryad Arbor) remaining a Land...Artifact Creature — Forest Borg. There's not near enough of these cards printed to concoct a deck which abuses the mechanical intricacies to the fullest, but even so we can get up to a bit of nonsense in turning things into Artifacts, or effects with specify 'non-[blank]' Creatures. There's been a few sets like Eldraine which care about non-Humans, and Assimilating something robs it of its humanity, so keep that in mind.

BPhillipYork: This is a neat way of handling the Borg, I still sort of wish they'd have a more Sliver like effect, or else something like Plague Rats. Nonetheless it's potentially a really strong reanimation type effect.

FromTheShire: Coming back from the dead as a stronger, mechanical, no longer human creature? Seems to capture the vibe of being Borgified to me. Unless you want to mess around with creature types there's nothing crazy here, and even if you do I'm not sure the juice is worth the squeeze, but at least you have the option.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

New Ability Words (Federation, Strange New Worlds, Battlefront, & Seek Out)

There's a host of new ability words appearing across the main & Commander sets, which delineate things such as drawing your second card, the number of differently named Lands you control, and more. Ability words don't affect gameplay, but do help guide players towards their specific payoff or theme, with Landfall being the gold standard for this text type.

Saffgor: Calling out differently-named Lands in the same set as a new type of Land token are introduced sure is a choice. Federation rewards you for tracking types in a way that flavorwise is a bit weird in Magic, where something like a Human Wizard Artificer is three types, and therefore the 'type=alien species' thing breaks down. That said, flavor is free, and I'm totally fine with them building on these shared conditions as the baseline of a set.

BPhillipYork: Federation is neat, though it's a bit strange that creature types like Klingon, Romulan, and Cardassian benefit Federation; I think part of the vision of Star Trek was that it wouldn't end up being a polar world with a continuum from good to bad. I think they did a good job with Federation matters and the Borg sub-type, and I think the way Federation works, benefiting from diversity essentially, is an example of a mechanic that fits the lore really well. I do think it's sad that they fixed the Werewolf Pack Leader thing. If you take that many steps you should be able to abuse Federation. Strange New Worlds to me really seems like a huge buff to green, which is the color best at ramping lands, and due to meta reasons it's already allowed a sort of unrestricted ramp that other colors are often not allowed. So far most of the cards that key off of it are pretty tame, but if they put too many ramp or extra land abilities keyed off of it it has the potential to get broken fast. Battlefront is an ability I really like, it encourages an active interactive game. It also pairs dangerous well with melee and myriad, and red+ decks running lots of these keywords will get aggressive really fast and be in your face, chipping down life totals very effectively. Which is good. Games should end. Seek Out is mostly a win more ability, though for red it's fairly easy to get additional draw that includes some discard, or else just run blue and draw a lot. However, I think Seek Out is a bit dangerous in that it benefits you even more from doing something that you basically want to do. It'll get pretty gross if you're able to trigger it on every turn, though like Ro Laren, Double Agent, you're dealing like 8 damage per cycle of turns, which isn't that impactful. I do think it's kind of interesting that every Seek Out card is a legendary creature.

Returning Mechanics

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Spacecraft & Station

Spacecraft is an Artifact subtype that allows you to tap Creatures you control as an activated ability to funnel their power into Charge counters, gaining cumulative effects based on the number of Charge counters accrued. Notably, Legendary Spacecraft (much like Vehicles) are legal as Commanders, something that we touched upon in last week's Commander Focus on the H.M.S. Bounty.

Saffgor: I've been in love with Spacecraft since the moment they debuted, having a Monogreen Spacecraft-matter deck in paper and now one helmed by the genuine article on the way (Happy ending, I bought the Bounty deck in paper). Spacecraft just succeed on every level, from flavor to function, and make for a compelling way to leverage tempo now for evasive power later. They play well, and it's the only reason I was remotely excited for Star Trek prior to its reveal. I'm glad that hype was paid off in full!

BPhillipYork: I feel like they did the whole Edge of Eternities set and the Spacecraft and Station abilities in order to make this set more palatable. Honestly. Nonetheless, these are fine and interesting mechanics, especially the way they dovetail with Commander, spaceship commanders ability to not be creatures then become creatures is really neat. I do think officers should be able to station better or something like that, missed opportunity.

FromTheShire: Behold the power of our fully operational subtype! I'm still not stoked about these existing in Magic from a flavor perspective, but I think they have done a great job with them mechanically and as expected we're getting a bunch of them here.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Planets & Land tokens

Planets originated as a cycle of 5 cards in Edge of Eternity as Lands with the ability to be Stationed, and return in Star Trek as...just another Land subtype, like Cave or Desert. Many cards in the set create Planet tokens instead of ramping normally, a new way to enable Landfall & token strategies, and pull upon a few of the Planet-matter cards in the set. Of note, the only Planets to have existed prior are the EOE cycle, and Planar Nexus.

Saffgor: A lot of the subtype's uniqueness has been robbed from it by not making these new Planets Station-able, but I get the concern over complexity. Landfall triggers are easier than ever now, and with quite a few of these Planet token producers being exceptionally playable, I think it's something we'll see a shift towards moving forward. After all, no searching means no shuffling, and that leads to better game pace.

BPhillipYork: These are also like, invented for this set and released in Edge of Eternities to keep the bitching about Universes Beyond to a minimum. Which is fine. They're fine. They won't be overly impactful in this set, planet tokens aren't overly useful with Strange new worlds since they are all named New Planet. Still they are kind of fun.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

Quests

A new cycle of quests arrive in Star Trek, originating in Zendikar and returning sporadically in a few recent Universes Beyond sets. With this new cycle, the number of Quest counter payoffs numbers 38, about as many Spacecraft that exist, so building around them feels within reach.

Saffgor: While I don't own it in paper, I do very often break out a Moira Brown, Guide Author deck online that's shockingly competent. With literally every release of new Quests, she becomes a better Commander, and frankly she was already pretty much there post-Avatar. Great to see these return as the 'heroic' counterpart to Marvel's Schemes.

BPhillipYork: This ability seems like a logical pairing given how much of Star Trek is about exploring strange new worlds and finding cool stuff.

Next Time: The Set’s Multicolor & Colorless Cards

That wraps up our look at the mechanics of Star Trek. We’ll be back later to look at the most noteworthy cards in the set, starting with the Multicolor and Colorless cards, and then Monocolor options in the following articles.

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@goonhammer.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? title: StarCraft: Tabletop Miniatures Game November 2026 FAQ - The Tabletop Battles Hot Take
content:
Archon has updated the FAQ document for StarCraft, issuing a solid number of new rulings and clarifications to help make sure everyone knows how the rules are intended to be played. And while most of these new entries do little more than clarifying that, yes, the rule actually means what it says, the added certainty the player base gets from having that clarification be set out is very welcome.

The oddest rulings here are a few around when models can overhang High Ground, likely necessitated by the addition of Siege Tanks and their massive bases with the last wave of releases. Beyond that, there’s about a page of new rulings you’ll need to be familiar with in your games going forward. Read on to see what’s been cleared up.

High Ground

First up, some entries about when a model’s base can hang off the edge of terrain. It’s now clarified that you can overhang the edge of High Ground if needed for Wobbly Model purposes, but just like situations where a model’s base can’t fit, the center of the base still has to be on the High Ground feature. But there’s nothing here that would let you overhang the edge if you’re not using the Wobbly Model Syndrome rules, so the number of situations where this would come up are pretty limited. Basically, if the movement rules would let you move a model somewhere its base can’t fit without hanging off the edge, you can still put it there so long as the center of its base is on the terrain feature. The most likely situation this would come up is a model that can only just barely make it to the top of one of one of the Lost Temple Ramp pieces. In such a circumstance, you’ll still be allowed to place it up there even if it’s not able to fit entirely on the terrain. But this rule won’t let you drive a siege tank up to the far edge of the terrain and voluntarily poke a tread out over it.

Credit: Contemptor Kevin Stillman

This update also clarifies that, if a model is overhanging the edge of a piece of High Ground terrain, no other models can go underneath it. This is probably for the best, as it keeps things as simple as possible when measuring range and line of sight.

Finally, an answer about when units on High Ground get to make an Evade roll: if every model in the defending unit has at least part of their base on High Ground, they’ll get the bonus. This means that if you had to take advantage of the first FAQ, you’ll still get the Evade roll.

Other Updates

General

The Artefact Hunt scenario card sees you carting objectives around the map to score, so people obviously wondered whether they could use abilities that let units teleport around the table to speed that process up. Previously, Archon had ruled that a unit carrying an objective marker could not use such an ability. They’ve since changed their minds: you can now use the ability, but you have to drop the objective marker first. This is a solid compromise and may create some interesting tension in your games: Protoss players can now use Adepts to pick up mission markers and try to run away, but if the enemy catches up to them they’ll have a decision to make: do they hope they can tough it out to keep moving the thing across the board, or do they save the unit at the cost of having to drop the marker?

Next up, an interesting question with a very confusing and not-too-helpful answer: if, between Surge rolls and Critical Hits, your opponent moves more dice from Armour straight to Damage than they actually rolled, does the Dodge ability actually do anything? Unfortunately, there’s no “yes” or “no” answer here, but we’re pretty sure the answer is yes. The ruling is that Surge and Critical Hit can’t move more dice out of the Armour pool than are actually there, and then seems to rule that Dodge then applies to reduce the number that are moved after you hit that limit. In other words, if we’re reading this right, Dodge always works to reduce the number of dice moved to a minimum of 0, regardless of how many dice your opponent moved.

Starcraft Terran Medic by Craig "MasterSlowPoke" Sniffen

What happens to rules that give a bonus to a weapon if you’re allowed to use that weapon twice? Well, as long as the bonus is still active, they keep it. The example given is comboing Khassar de Templari with the Gateway’s Quick Strikes: the unit’s first Combat Weapon will have Precision (2) both times you use it, not just the first. This one could have gone either way, but this is a fine answer that is consistent with the rules as written.

Finally, a ruling that’s very straightforward but might be a little unintuitive: how does Concentrated Fire (X) affect units that already had damage assigned? Well, the rule does what it says: after you destroy the maximum number of models you’re allowed to, all remaining damage is removed. Since the rules don’t care about where damage came from, once a weapon with this rule had killed all the models it’s allowed to kill, any leftovers are discarded.

There are also a slew of really simple clarifications that are nonetheless nice to have definitive answers on:

  • Tactical cards and special abilities don’t require line of sight unless they explicitly say so, even if they only work within a specified range.
  • A Hold action is an action, and resolving it will trigger any effects that key off of completing an action.
  • On the other hand, passing the phase does not count as an action, and won’t trigger any of those effects.
  • Area-of-effect abilities ignore elevation unless explicitly stated otherwise. And yes, this means Creep climbs up walls, and that you can spread new Creep tumors to High Ground ignoring elevation changes.
  • Impact (X) does not actually target anything, so it sidesteps abilities that prevent units from being targeted. This is mostly important right now because it means Impact hits can, in fact, damage structures.
  • The Indomitable rule means what it says, and so engaged units that have it can’t target or be targeted by engaged enemies, even if those enemies also have Indomitable.

Zerg

Three Zerg-specific clarifications, none of which are particularly unexpected.

Credit: Blizzard Entertainment/Archon Studios
  • Ravagers’ Corrosive Bile ability gets a clarification: since it’s not actually targeting a unit, you don’t check line of sight for purposes of removing casualties. This means that a unit will take all the damage you roll from the ability if they’re in range, regardless of whether they tried to hide behind cover.
  • The Omega Worm’s ability to deploy units from its base (as well as Zagara’s, when she releases shortly) still counts as having been used for deployment purposes if you measure from it for Burrow Ambush. Seems like an obvious ruling, but a good one to have.
  • As we mentioned above, Creep tokens only care about horizontal distance when you’re spreading Creep across the table.

Terran

There are a handful of clarifications here:

Boom, baby! - Starcraft Terran Marauder by Craig "MasterSlowPoke" Sniffen
  • The Griffin Support ability on the new Nova Covert Ops Faction card doesn’t actually target a friendly unit, so you can measure the 12” to drop the Sabotage Drone from any friendly model. And yes, this explicitly includes Nova’s Holo Decoy. Cute.
  • The Sabotage Drone itself here catches a very situational nerf: the Zerg Bile Launcher doesn’t actually take the extra hits, presumably because it has the “Biological Structure” ability and not the “Structure” ability. While that may be true as written, it’s honestly weird and limits the utility of the thing into Zerg players. We hope they reconsider this (or errata the drone itself to also apply to “Biological Structures”).
  • Multiple Siege Tanks can use the Coordinated Strike ability on the same friendly spotter, but only the most recent one to use it can benefit from it. Solid ruling that will help ensure that a potentially powerful ability doesn’t get out of hand.
  • Killing a Raven doesn’t turn off Explosive Shrapnel Shells or Seeker Missile. This is expected, but also keep in that Seeker Missile won’t go off if the target moved and the Raven is dead, regardless of where it was before you killed it.

Protoss

These ones are a little weirder, but most of them work like they ought to if you think through the rules. The final clarification about High Templar is one that I honestly wouldn’t know how to rule without this answer, though, so I’m glad it made it to print well in advance of the unit showing up on the table.

Artanis
  • The Nerazim Faction card’s Might of the Nerazim reaction is triggered immediately when a unit loses Hidden. That means that a unit of Stalkers affected by Path of Shadows can pick up Critical Hit (2) from that card when they lose hidden by performing a ranged attack action.
  • Only the currently-active unit can use activated abilities, so if you use Khassar de Templari on the Templar Caste faction card to take an action with a different unit, the other unit you chose can’t use its abilities.
  • On the other hand, the unit you activated to trigger Khassar de Templari can use any activated abilities it has, even though it doesn’t get to actually make an action.
  • When High Templar release, Psionic Storm’s blast template has to be placed “center-to-center” over the token you use to mark where it will be.

Final Thoughts

With the exception of the High Ground clarifications (which are a little weird, likely due to the fact that they’re covering a real edge case), most of these clarifications are straightforward and make sense given how the rules are written.

To be clear, that’s a good thing: answering questions the community has is a great way to make sure that everyone knows how the game is meant to be played, and equips all players to have a consistent and fun play experience regardless of where they are. While there are one or two changes we think they ought to revisit (“Biological Structures” aren’t “Structures”? Really?), the fact they’re not afraid to put the answers to these questions in writing where everyone can have access to them is a great sign.

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: Warhammer Survivors is a reheated clone, but I'm still playing the $#!% out of it
content:
Our Verdict

Not much more than a clone of Vampire Survivors with the Warhammer 40k and Warhammer: Age of Sigmar licenses, it's at least a good copy of a good game, and the Warhammer paintjob has been applied with care and attention. Not in the least innovative, but a very enjoyable comfort game with a lot of replay value.

Pros
  • Low-stress comfort gaming
  • Dopamine fireworks show
  • Gorgeous Warhammer pixel art
  • Loads of secrets to unearth
Cons
  • Vampire Survivors already exists
  • Addictive
  • Conceivably an epilepsy risk

 

 

At its mechanical core, Warhammer Survivors is a near-clone of 2021's Vampire Survivors, set in the Warhammer 40k and Warhammer Age of Sigmar universes. Fans of the original bullet heaven game will find precious little new here, but the dopamine spewing special effects and meta-progression that made the original a 100 hour hit are as addictive as ever.

Publisher Auroch Digital provided me with a review key for Warhammer Survivors, but a board game review and a trip to Berlin meant I only started playing it yesterday. I thought I would have to delay this review to get enough playtesting time in - that was before the addictive gameplay loop got its teeth into me, and I logged twelve hours in two sittings.

If your gaming diet for the last five years has consisted solely of miniature wargames and perhaps the odd Warhammer 40k game on PC or console, you might have missed Vampire Survivors and the 'bullet-heaven' genre it spawned. The first half of this review describes the basic gameplay of the genre, but if you're already familiar with it, skip ahead to where I talk about what's different in Warhammer Survivors.

There isn't much. Warhammer Survivors is so close to its inspiration that I can clue you in to the basic mechanics for both games in the same description. In fact, I'm not even going to refer to Warhammer for the next eight paragraphs.

How does Warhammer Survivors play? Like Vampire Survivors

You control a tiny pixellated dude in the middle of an unfeasibly huge map. Pixellated enemies spawn in continuously, and you'll attack them automatically. The only thing you have to worry about is movement, skilfully navigating the ever-growing maze of mobs to preserve your health and get into position so each attack deals maximum damage.

Defeated enemies drop XP gems, which you need to physically collect. This adds a little bit of risk and reward, a need to balance your short term safety against your long term XP gain, as you dart around mobs that inevitably pile up on top of the treasure.

XP means level ups, and level-ups mean upgrades, giving you new weapons and passive support items or levelling up your existing kit. The enemies get stronger too, periodically spawning even tougher bosses who drop treasure chests full of more loot when they die. Carefully selecting synergistic upgrades is key to passing the ever-more-difficult DPS checks the game throws at you - but you'll inevitably die, long short of the time limit for the level.

You'll likely be holding a hoard of gold at this point, found in destructible environmental objects and inside treasure chests. Between runs you can spend this cash on upgrades to your stats or to unlock new characters once you discover them in maps or by achieving certain milestones. Then you go again, and hopefully hang on a little longer.

That's a simple but already compelling core. The auto-attack system isn't mindless, as every weapon has its own finicky positioning or targeting controls: weapons that attack horizontally can't reach enemies above or below you, weapons that attack the closest foe struggle to focus-fire single targets in mobs, powerful attacks on long cool-downs need support from smaller weapons to clear paths for you to move through when the screen inevitably fills up before they can fire again.

The game is also rife with secrets. Kill a boss while holding a level 10 weapon and the correct support item, and its treasure chest will contain an evolved form of that weapon. These have higher damage output you never thought possible and explosive special FX. Every weapon has a unique combo piece to discover, and they're not always synergistic, pushing your builds into strange directions as you chase the evolved weapons you need to make it to the end of a run.

With a powerful enough build you'll make it to the final five minutes of the level and a casino of vibrant FX, numbers, dings, and other feedback. Getting to this hyperactive final phase reveals the pixel art as not just an aesthetic choice, but what allows a regular games console or mid-range PC to render this many objects on screen.

Make it all the way to the end of the level and you'll face off against an extreme mega-boss who is initially unkillable. Of course there's a secret way to bring them down, you've just got to find out. At the end of a good run you'll be faced with a cascade of trophies and tick-boxes as you discover all the 'firsts' you achieved, which in turn unlock new items, new characters to purchase, new levels, faster play modes, more secrets…

So it was written in Vampire Survivors, so it is in Warhammer Survivors. I don't use the term "clone" lightly, but mechanically this is extremely close to the same game. The setting is different, and what mechanical differences exist between the two games stem from the setting - and the choice for that to be two settings.

Two games in one

Warhammer Survivors has two modes, Warhammer 40k and Warhammer: Age of Sigmar. Though mechanically identical, each has a distinct roster of characters, distinct levels, distinct enemies, distinct weapons, distinct achievements and unlocks. The only thing persistent between them is the gold you earn in levels and whichever global stat boosts you spend it on - otherwise, they're two separate games.

This occasionally feels like an artificial separation. Support items, and a class of fourth-wall breaking weapons that includes pots of Nuln Oil paint or hurtling D6s, are shared between the two games, but achievements connected to those items aren't. There are a lot of unlocks that rely on getting an item to level six in a run, and you'll need to do that in both games to make the same progress. It's busywork.

Still, swapping from one world to the other is quite refreshing. The game has two weapon pools tailored to two enemy sets, two different levels, and if you get frustrated in one mode you can hop into the other. I've yet to unlock it, but there's also a painting desk map which breaks the fourth wall entirely, acknowledges that these warriors are all toy soldiers, and allows enemies from both universes to freely mix and match.

A small but substantive mechanical difference from Vampire Survivors comes from the inclusion of Followers. Not every weapon you can find can be used by every character, but this doesn't remove them from the item pool. Collecting them sees your character joined by another hero, maybe a Space Marine, or Sister of Battle or Stormcast Eternal, to wield the weapon in an IP-approved manner.

This second sprite doesn't take damage but does become the point of origin for the weapon, which creates subtle new tactical possibilities. Sister Superior Amelia Novena projects a damaging Aura of Faith. Playing as her puts you dead center of a zone that fries weak enemies; when you get a Sister of Battle follower she and the aura trail behind your character. You're more vulnerable to enemies in your path, but if you're skirting the edges of a mob you can get the aura deeper into the press.

The developers also use your follower count as a new tool for differentiating characters and weapons. The Cadian Trooper Bartosz Kozlowski gets a boost to their experience gain rate the more followers are with them, while the Witch Hunter Callis gets additional attacks when he has exactly one follower, a nod to the fact he's usually paired up with his buddy Toll in novels and on the tabletop. Fielding a party containing both of them even unlocks a cosmetic for the pair.

For all that Warhammer Survivors is little more than a clone, I can't call that a damning criticism. I really liked Vampire Survivors. I am an absolute rube for this kind of dopamine-spaffing fireworks factory.

If you played Vampire Survivors, you want to do it all over again from the beginning without resetting your account, and you like Warhammer, you'll enjoy this. If you're new to the bullet heaven genre and you like Warhammer, this is an easy recommend - just remember to come up for air from time to time.

Playing Warhammer Survivors has me fiending for some recommendations for more modern bullet heaven games that push the genre forwards. If you've got any, I'd love to hear them in the Wargamer Discord community.
